title: Chapter 169: Door!
html:
“Everything about this child fascinates me, yet I fear learning too much. He is like a swamp: the closer one approaches, the louder one’s instincts sound the alarm.

“His mother has bipolar disorder and remains calm only in his presence. To support her treatment, the doctors often bring him to visit. Every child depends naturally upon its mother. Small as he is, he recognizes her.

“The strangest moment came when he saw her. His first word was neither ‘Mama’ nor his own name, but ‘door.’

“At first, I thought I had misheard a meaningless sound. But as the nurse carried him away, he pointed one tiny finger toward his mother’s door and repeated the word—door.

“He seemed desperate to approach it. I questioned the entire staff, and not one person had taught him that word.

“Without instruction, he pronounced it and understood its meaning. Who taught him? Is something else living inside this hospital?

“Then matters grew stranger. When a nurse and I carried him into Room 3, he looked down the empty corridor and waved as though greeting someone.

“That alone might not have alarmed me, but the nurse noticed too. She asked what he was doing and whom he saw.

“The child stammered a name—He Yajun.

“The nurse assumed he was merely practicing sounds and carried him away. I wanted desperately to stop her, because He Yajun had been a real person: a construction worker killed in an accident before the Third Sick Hall was completed.

“Even the doctors and nurses did not know that history. How had the child learned his name?

“I watched from the doorway as the nurse carried him upstairs. Once again, he waved toward an empty corner. I have treated many mentally ill children and never felt afraid. That day, in that corridor, terror seized me.

“After that incident, I paid closer attention to the boy.”

The first letter ended there without identifying its intended recipient. The salutation—Doctor Chen—was the only clue.

Surname Chen? Could it be Dad? But he’s a Haunted House operator, not a doctor!

For a moment, he thought he had found a clue to his father. Reflection tempered that optimism. He opened the second letter, whose contents were even more extraordinary.

“Doctor Chen, we have to meet in person. Things are getting slightly out of control.

“Once the child learned to crawl, he began seeking his mother. No one in the Third Sick Hall understood how he escaped the office and reached Room 3 alone.

“The other staff have noticed his strange behavior. He rarely cries, smiles at empty spaces, and grows more excited as darkness falls. He does not behave like an ordinary child.

“His ability to learn is extraordinary. Though still very young, he speaks clearly—yet his words often chill everyone who hears them.

“Perhaps the world looks different through his eyes. He treats sedated patients like toys and watches them as though they were already dead.

“He waves at patients who have lost touch with reality but never looks at their faces. Instead, he stares above their shoulders, as if something sits there.

“Strangest of all, he sits outside Room 3 for hours. He never enters, only stares at the door. Some doctors and nurses want him sent to an orphanage because he frightens them. But removing him would jeopardize his mother’s recovery, which took a year to stabilize. We cannot give up now.

“I rejected the suggestion. Several months later, the police brought good news. Tracing the car’s license plate, they found the boy’s biological father in the south. By then, the mother had nearly recovered. We hired a lawyer and took the man to court, demanding payment of the outstanding fees and legal recognition of both mother and child.

“We won. Whether guilt or fear of prison changed him, I cannot say. The mother continued improving and displayed remarkable strength in her son’s presence.

“After another six months, her condition fully stabilized. She had few friends or relatives, so only several doctors saw them off. The child left with her, though three years in the hospital had already scarred him. On his final night, he slipped back into the corridor and whispered incomprehensible words to the door.

“I believed the ordeal finished when they left. I never imagined events would take such an unexpected turn.

“One year later, when the child was four, his father brought him back to the center.

“The man said the mother had been murdered at home and the boy witnessed everything. When I saw him again, he had changed completely. The only pillar in his life had collapsed, leaving him much as his mother had been upon admission.

“Given their history, we refused to admit him and urged his father to use a public hospital. That night, precisely at midnight, blood began seeping from Room 3’s white door.

“It continued for exactly one minute. I learned of the incident a week later, after many unbelievable events had already occurred.”

The second letter ended abruptly. Its description reminded Chen Ge of someone who had endured precisely that childhood.

He tore open the third envelope and found a photograph of mother and son. Emotion surged through him: he had seen this same picture while helping Doctor Gao pack Men Nan’s belongings at Hai Ming Apartments.

A woman in a hospital gown leaned against the bed, a shy little boy seated beside her.
